The gray rectangular conductor is located in the xy plane, and black dots are drawn around it and within the conductor region, indicating that the magnetic field B points toward +z. The power supply symbol is below, with + marked on the left side, indicating that the positive terminal of the power supply is connected to the left side of the conductor, and the right side is connected to the other end. Then reason: the positive terminal of the power supply is on the left side, so the ordinary driving electric field inside the conductor is along the direction from left to right, that is, the +x direction. In metal, the charge carriers are electrons, and the electron drift direction is opposite to the conventional current direction, so the electron drift velocity points toward -x. The magnetic field is +z, so the magnetic force received by the electrons is in the -y direction, causing negative charge to accumulate on the lower side of the conductor. The transverse electric field produced by the Hall effect points toward the side where negative charge accumulates, that is, the -y direction. Therefore, the electric field inside the conductor has two components: one along +x, and the other along -y.

method.method_draft: First read the diagram: the coordinate axes show +x to the right, +y upward, and +z out of the page; the magnetic field is drawn as dots through the gray conductor, so B is in +z. The source has its + terminal on the left side of the circuit and the opposite terminal on the right, so the ordinary driving electric field through the conductor is from left to right, i.e. +x. Then use the electron Hall-effect picture: in a metal, electrons drift opposite the conventional current, so their drift velocity is toward -x. With B in +z, the magnetic force on the drifting electrons is toward -y, causing negative charge to build up on the lower side of the conductor. The Hall electric field therefore points toward that negative side, giving an electric-field component in -y. Combine the driving field and Hall field: E has components in +x and -y.

method.method_draft: Read from the figure that +x is rightward, +y is upward, B is represented by dots and is therefore +z, and the battery places higher potential on the left side of the conductor than the right. The longitudinal Ohmic field is therefore E_x in the +x direction. For the transverse component, use the steady-state Hall/Drude balance for electrons with no net current in the y direction: the Hall field must cancel the magnetic part of the carrier force. Since the conventional current density is along +x, electron drift is along -x; equivalently, for electron carriers the Hall field direction follows E_H = (j × B)/(ne). With j along +x and B along +z, j × B points in -y. Thus the transverse electric-field component is -y, while the longitudinal component is +x.
